overview.text: Abstract art is an approach that gives line, color, shape, texture, and form greater emphasis than realistic depiction of a subject. It is not one uniform style: some artists simplify things observed in nature, while others make images with no recognizable subject. This freedom lets artists use visual choices to communicate mood, ideas, or personal experience rather than merely copy appearances. In early twentieth-century America, Arthur Dove developed abstract forms from landscapes and natural cycles; later, Abstract Expressionists explored both energetic gestures and expansive fields of color. The movement’s first generation flourished between 1943 and the mid-1950s, helping shift the postwar art world’s focus from Paris to New York.

key_facts.text: Abstract art does not depict its subject in a realistic way; it emphasizes visual elements such as line, color, shape, texture, and form.
Abstraction can simplify recognizable subjects: Arthur Dove drew on landscapes and used expressive color and line to reduce them to essential forms.
The Met describes Dove as an early American abstract artist and says he is considered the first American artist to make purely nonrepresentational imagery.
Abstract Expressionism included energetic, gestural painting as well as reflective works focused on broad fields of color.
The first generation of Abstract Expressionists flourished from 1943 to the mid-1950s; the movement helped shift the postwar art world’s focus from Paris to New York.
